judge_assessment.explanation: The corrections are all mathematically right and I recomputed each: y = 3(4)+5 = 17; y = 12-2(5) = 2; slope (11-3)/(6-2) = 2 against Dev's inverted 1/2; the table steps by 4; the hidden intercept is 13-4 = 9; b = 20-4(3) = 8 giving y = 4x+8; and the pool's rate is (22-46)/(8-2) = -4 with b = 46-(-4)(2) = 54, checked against the second reading (-4(8)+54 = 22). Every planted error does target the requested slope-versus-intercept distinction, as the judge says, and each wrong value is declared as trap data in verify.json rather than typed into the stem by hand. Two claims are broader than the artifacts support. 'Exactly eight readable find-and-fix problems are present' is true, but the coverage is not: every problem prints an (a) part and a (b) part, and verify.json covers only the (b) parts. Problem 1(a) asks the student to 'State the real slope and the real y-intercept' - the answers 3 and 5, both trivially machine-checkable - and there is no entry for them; verify.json id 1 is a lone eval of 3(4)+5. Problem 6(a) asks the student to 'Test Owen's equation at x = 3 and say what it gives', and the key answers it in full (4(3)+20 = 32), but no verify entry produces 32; instead id 6 carries two entries that both produce 8 (an eval y-mx and a solve for b), so the bank row reads '6. 8, 8' for a problem whose two printed slots are 32 and 8. The worksheet's own directions say 'In each problem: name the error in words first, then show corrected work', which makes a naming-the-error slot on all seven of problems 1-7; the only manual entry in the file is id 8. So on a sheet whose instructional mode is misconception analysis, seven diagnoses are recorded as machine-verified and one grading row is misleading.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 4 and 5 are a designed pair on one table: problem 4 establishes the step size of 4, and problem 5 then requires working backwards one step from the x=1 row to reach the intercept 9 - which forces the student to confront that the table never shows x=0. The stem of 5 even says 'Using the step size of 4 you found in problem 4', so the dependency is explicit rather than assumed.

Every misconception is declared as machine-checked trap data with the exact number a confused student produces: 23 from 5(4)+3 on problem 1, 58 on problem 2, 0.5 on problem 3, 13 on problems 4 and 5, 20 on problem 6, and -0.25 and 46 on problem 7. The distractor printed in the stem and the value flagged in verify.json cannot drift apart.

Problem 7 is the strongest item: both of the student's reported numbers are wrong, and the key ties them to one root confusion rather than two ('the two errors are the same mistake twice: a number that belongs to one particular moment was used as though it described the whole relationship'), then checks the repaired model against the second reading.

Problem 8's manual entry is a usable rubric rather than a placeholder: it names the objective criterion for full credit ('any argument that identifies slope as a rate of change per unit of x and the y-intercept as the single output at x equal to zero'), and the three sub-parts (a), (b), (c) each ask for a different form of the same distinction.

root_causes.description: Verification was planned one entry per problem's terminal computation, but every problem on this sheet prints two lettered slots. The (a) slots - which are where the misconception is actually named or tested - were left uncovered even when they are ordinary machine-checkable values (problem 1(a)'s slope and intercept, problem 6(a)'s 32). Because the Quick Answers bank is generated from verify.json, problem 6's row prints the same value twice and nothing for the slot the student answers first.

improvements.title: Cover the (a) slots: declare problem 1's slope and intercept and problem 6's test value 32
improvements.proposed_change: Build the response-slot inventory from lettered sub-parts as well as conjoined imperatives, and fail the build when a printed slot has no bound entry. For this case add eval entries for problem 1(a) (m = 3 and b = 5) and for problem 6(a) (m*x + b at m=4, b=20, x=3 -> 32). Also have render_quick_answers order and, where a problem has lettered parts, label the values by sub-part, so problem 6's row reads '(a) 32, (b) 8' instead of '8, 8'.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: problem 6's stem with its two lettered parts and this task's verify.json id 6 (two entries both expecting 8). The slot check must exit non-zero naming the uncovered 6(a) slot; after adding the eval that yields 32, the fixture passes and the rendered bank row must contain 32 as well as 8. Today the row is '8, 8' and no assertion on 32 can succeed.
improvements.expected_impact: Fixes a grading row that currently prints one problem's answer twice while omitting the other, and closes the coverage gap on the halves of these problems where the misconception is actually tested.
improvements.risk: Sub-part splitting will occasionally treat a rhetorical (a) ('Explain why ...') as a machine slot; those must route to manual entries rather than forcing an invented numeric check.

improvements.title: Require a manual entry for the named-error slot on each of problems 1-7
improvements.proposed_change: Add the open-response scan to the gate chain and, for misconception-analysis mode specifically, state in SKILL.md that the diagnosis is always a manual slot even when the correction is machine-verified. On this sheet that means seven manual entries alongside the existing numeric checks - which is the honest picture of an error-analysis worksheet, not an inflated one. references/manual-review-aid.md should be cited in the same rule so the review load stays workable.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture with problem 3's stem ('(a) Say which change Dev put on top, and which one belongs there. (b) Find the correct slope.') and a verify.json id 3 holding only the slope entry. The check must exit non-zero naming the (a) diagnosis slot; adding a manual entry makes it pass and raises the run exit code from 0 to 2.
improvements.expected_impact: On a sheet whose entire instructional mode is diagnosis, the diagnoses stop being invisible to review. It also makes the manual count reflect reality: today the artifact reports one reviewable item for a worksheet that asks for eight explanations.
improvements.risk: Seven manual items on an eight-problem sheet looks like a regression in automation and will lower the machine-verified ratio in run statistics; that ratio is measuring the wrong thing for this mode and the reporting should say so.

case_summary: A precise slope-versus-intercept error-analysis packet: all seven corrections are mathematically right, every planted wrong value is declared as trap data so the stem and the verifier cannot drift apart, problems 4 and 5 form a deliberate pair on one table that forces the student to notice the table never shows x = 0, and problem 8 carries a genuine rubric. The gap is coverage. Every problem prints an (a) and a (b) slot and verify.json covers only (b): problem 1(a)'s slope 3 and intercept 5 have no entry, and problem 6(a)'s test value 32 has none either - instead id 6 carries two entries that both yield 8, so the bank row reads '6. 8, 8' for a problem whose printed answers are 32 and 8. The worksheet's own directions require naming the error in words on all seven diagnostic problems, yet the only manual entry is on problem 8, so seven diagnoses are recorded as machine-verified on a misconception-analysis sheet.
